extracted.intended_audience: writers, humorists, critics, and students of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles for composing and judging jokes/humorous writing, with emphasis on poetic vs. practical humor and the conditions that make a joke 'good' or 'bad'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic humor (vs. practical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic jokes provoke laughter without a point and often rely on vivid, incongruous imagery or on seeing the world from another point of view; they can provoke laughter 'without a point' and are more enduring than practical jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic humor rests on the imagination's sympathy and the ability to perceive familiar things in new, incongruous ways (examples: re-naming Turner's painting, an elephant 'walking as though his pants were coming down'). When poetic incongruities fail, the poet can fall back on the crude flow of materials and horse-play: the mere presentation of queer combinations of attributes may suffice. Poetic humor often tickles more strongly than mere vacancy of meaning because it presents an actual thing rather than absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law Number One — Engagement of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a real engagement of the interest of the person who is expected to laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is a feeling and play instinct; jokes cannot strongly affect unless the audience's voluntary nature is alert. Both the direction of the disappointment and that of the satisfaction must be interesting. Avoid relying on purely 'logical' or 'cerebral' forms of laughter; ensure material is interesting to the audience. Techniques to conform include attributing jokes to prominent personalities or to one's own past to provide warmth and personality, but use these with courage and preparedness (beware being contradicted: 'Yes, I heard that story up in Montreal'). 'Humor must be alive' — avoid perfunctory or 'kiddding' that trusts mere comical form to produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Richness — two strong currents of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A rich joke is 'a poetic-practical joke in which the interest balked and the one satisfied are both strong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good/rich jokes require at least two strongly flowing currents of interest in the listener (both for and against, or both disappointed expectation and corresponding satisfaction). Examples: marriage jokes (because audience feelings are mixed), the 'appendix removed twice' anecdote (reinforced point). Topics whose audience feelings flow strongly only in one direction (e.g., mothers-in-law) are less often 'rich.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Law Number Two — Appropriate emotional intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The feelings aroused in the person who is expected to laugh must not be too strong and deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is play; some topics provoke passions or grief too deep to be playfully treated — jokes about matters of intense feeling can become tragedies if mistimed. Avoid malapropos or untimely jokes. Hostile jokes carried too far and obscene/sexual jokes can be inappropriate because they touch deep passions or regress to infantile contempt. Courage is required to jest in grave circumstances (e.g., death-bed jests by morally robust figures), but most cannot safely do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law Number Three — Natural induction of negative and positive currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the negative (interest balked) and the positive (satisfaction) currents of feeling must be simply and naturally induced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke must not seem artificial, manufactured, dragged in, far-fetched, or labored. There must be no appearance of effort in building up the interest or planting the seed of satisfaction. Labored attempts kill humor (example: Mark Twain's famously labored speech that failed to provoke laughter). Avoid showing the 'hard labor' of joke construction; humor should appear to arise spontaneously like a wild bird from a natural pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law Number Four — Immediate and perfect identity of disappointment and satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the positive current with the negative must be immediate and perfect; the satisfaction must be in the disappointment with no mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The point must flash instantaneously; brevity and immediacy are essential ('brevity is the soul of wit'). You cannot explain a joke; explanation or mediation kills it. Avoid forced jokes where the audience must infer or bridge the point (examples: strained Shakespearean lines and the clown's 'Why, here in Denmark' — these require pretense or force and thus are imperfect). Translated or transported jokes often become forced when their linguistic or cultural identity is not immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of attribution/persona to increase interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Imputing a joke to a prominent personality or to one's own past can increase the audience's engagement and tolerance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributing material to figures like Mark Twain colors a joke with authority and personality and can 'tune it up' to a better explosion; attributing it to one's own history gives it visible warmth. These tricks must be used with preparedness and courage because being contradicted can expose the artifice. They are strategies to satisfy Law One (engagement).
